abstract: An opening salvo of lawsuits in US courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: Product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and postdeployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: Trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor's responsibility by their intent's specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology's pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Where intention goes, responsibility flows: Grounding AI accountability in the machine learning paradigm

abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase

abstract: Achieving reliable, remote control over multiple stable states in modular systems remains a challenge due to the coupling between modules and history-dependent transitions. Here, we present magnetic origami state machines that enable deterministic navigation from any unknown initial state to any target state under magnetic actuation. By assuming mutually distinct energy barriers in modular Kresling origami assemblies, we realize fully accessible transition graphs with scalable state spaces. Guided by the graph associated to the state machine, a rotating magnetic field induces a universal reset that autonomously drives the system to a known equilibrium state from arbitrary states without sensing or feedback, while pulsed magnetic inputs further enable programmable transitions to any target state via prescribed actuation sequences. A reduced-order Lagrangian mechanics model predicts snap-through dynamics across reset, stepwise programming (between graph nodes), and shortcuts (by adapting pulse magnitude and orientation) where inertia triggers simultaneous multicell transitions with a single pulse. These results establish a general framework for programmable magneto-mechanical state machines with autonomous state reset and full state-space control.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Origami state machine with time-varying magnetic fields

abstract: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder-noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder-noncrowder interactions and all crowder-crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Multiscale Brownian dynamics simulations reveal effects of macromolecular crowding on protein–ligand association

abstract: Nitrogen-fixing root nodules develop as lateral organs on legume roots and their formation is restricted by autoregulation of nodulation (AON), a systemic mechanism with unclear evolutionary origins. We identify Lotus japonicus NUCLEAR FACTOR Y subunit A4 ( NF-YA4 ) gene as a central target of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase HAR1, which controls both AON and root system architecture. Under nonsymbiotic conditions, HAR1 suppresses expression of NF-YA4 and its close paralog NF-YA1 , at least in part through a miR169-dependent mechanism, mirroring the Arabidopsis CLAVATA1/2-miR169- NF-YA module. Loss of HAR1 leads to NF-YA4 overexpression, broad transcriptional reprogramming, and induction of LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN , STYLISH , and YUCCA auxin biosynthesis genes, enhancing auxin signaling and lateral root development. Grafting experiments show that HAR1 constrains NF-YA4 -mediated branching both locally in roots and systemically from shoots. Because NF-YA4 functions partly redundantly with NF-YA1 to mediate nodule emergence, our results suggest a model in which duplication and neofunctionalization of an ancestral NF-YA-dependent pathway controlling lateral root development facilitated its recruitment to the nodulation program. They also raise the possibility that AON could have evolved, at least in part, through the co-option of a LRR-RK/miR169/ NF-YA regulatory module that limited lateral root development.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: HAR1 receptor kinase links nodule autoregulation with repression of auxin signaling and lateral root development

abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling

abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to "open" and "closed" architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase

abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin's protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin's retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose-response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling

abstract: Recently, we lost one of the original developers of the field of molecular electronics. Mark A. Ratner wrote a famous paper in 1974 that developed the theoretical framework for making a molecule act as a rectifier. This idea, and a host of further ideas that were stimulated by this and other papers, led to a huge amount of experimental and theoretical studies that continue to this day. But Mark's career was much more than that, with leadership at Northwestern University and beyond that continues to shape the scientific enterprise.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Mark A. Ratner (1942–2026): Founded molecular electronics while spearheading the growth of science at Northwestern University

abstract: Two-dimensional superconductors, including twisted multilayer graphene, should exhibit a BKT transition, and the $T$-dependence of the superfluid stiffness should distinguish between nodal or gapped order parameter symmetries. However, this picture dramatically changes when spatially correlated disorder is taken into account. Such correlations naturally arise in moiré systems due to twist angle inhomogeneities, which we model using elasticity theory. Using a random impedance network based on realistic disorder in the local $T_c$, we show that the finite-frequency conductance reveals a smeared percolative transition instead of a BKT transition. At low temperatures, the disorder can effectively obscure the distinction between nodal and fully gapped superconducting order parameters. We propose that the real part of the conductivity can be used as a key diagnostic observable to probe the relevance of correlated disorder.
title: How twist angle inhomogeneity masks the superconducting order parameter symmetry

abstract: The discovery of superconducting nickelates provides a unique opportunity to explore the pairing mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity. Here, we use ultrafast terahertz spectroscopy to probe the temperature-dependent superfluid density in an infinite-layer samarium nickelate film with a Tc of 20 K. The superfluid density decreases linearly with rising temperature, consistent with clean limit d-wave pairing. From this linear relation, we extract a superconducting gap of 2.5 meV and a gap-to-Tc ratio of 3, suggesting that this sample lies in the weak-coupling limit. Furthermore, the ratio of the mean free path to the coherence length, is determined to be 1.5, confirming the clean-limit behavior. These findings establish strong parallels between the pairing mechanisms in nickelate and cuprate superconductors.
title: Evidence for clean d-wave superconductivity in the samarium nickelates

abstract: The two-to-two four-dimensional scattering amplitude of identical scalars obeys rigorous two-sided non-perturbative bounds derived via the modern numerical S-matrix bootstrap. These bounds carve out an allowed region with a rich boundary structure, featuring edges and vertices. In this work we further tighten this region and uncover the physics of its boundary by analyzing the asymptotic Regge behavior of the amplitude and the spectrum of resonances and virtual states. We find that the S-matrices along a given edge exhibit universal behavior, sharply contrasting with that on other edges. This reveals a classification of the boundary into distinct phases, corresponding to different UV mechanisms by which a gapped scalar arises.
title: Phases of the scalar S -matrix island

abstract: Microbes in marine environments are often confined to thin near-surface layers while being advected by turbulent flows. Because such constrained advection generates an effectively compressible flow, reproduction and transport interact in a nontrivial way. Here, we focus on populations whose growth is governed by an Allee effect and show that sinks and sources, generated by the compressible flow, have dramatic consequences for the survival of such species. We derive analytical expressions for the carrying capacity as a function of the Allee strength in the limit of small and large Damköhler number, which measures the product of the large eddy turnover time and the organism growth rate. Numerical simulations reveal how these two limits connect. In the limit of small Damköhler number, we find a maximal Allee strength, set by the statistics of the compressible flow, that leads to species extinction in fully developed turbulence.
title: Allee effect in compressible flows

abstract: It is a widely accepted paradigm that collisionless magnetic reconnection proceeds at a universal fast rate of $\sim0.1$ when normalized to a properly defined reconnecting magnetic field and Alfvén speed, effectively independent of the macroscopic system size. This conclusion, derived primarily from kinetic simulations of classical Harris current sheets with kinetic-scale thickness, stands in contrast to results from forced reconnection and island coalescence, where the rate significantly depends on the system size. Here, we reconcile this disparity by performing a rigorous scaling study using both particle-in-cell and Hall magnetohydrodynamic simulations. We demonstrate that when the global magnetic configuration is self-consistently preserved by scaling the initial current sheet thickness proportionally with the system size, the ``universal'' fast rate disappears. Instead, the reconnection rate decreases as the system size increases. These results indicate that dependence on macroscopic scales is not peculiar to specific geometries but is a fundamental property of collisionless reconnection, effectively unifying the Harris sheet with other configurations exhibiting size-dependence.
title: System size dependence of collisionless reconnection rate
